text:
Recommendation: run a six-week, hands-on maker programme called Teen Makers Lab for 12 teens aged 13 to 17, meeting for 90 minutes each Thursday, with a single librarian facilitating and a small volunteer team handling snacks and tech support. Participants build a short tangible project each week (a cardboard arcade game, a simple circuit with a light or buzzer, a stop-motion or podcast episode), and reading and writing enter through the project brief rather than as a set text. Non-reading teens come because the room is a place to make things with friends and to get a finished product, not a place to read.

Week-by-week plan: Week 1, introductions and a build-a-badge circuit kit (about $15 per kit, shared in pairs). Week 2, cardboard arcade machine design with a written game rulebook. Week 3, podcast recording of a 5-minute episode on a topic the group chooses, with scripting and editing. Week 4, stop-motion animation with a written storyboard. Week 5, peer showcase where teens present their work to families and friends. Week 6, a graduation session with certificates, a take-home zine of the group's work, and a library card sign-up. Each session runs 90 minutes with a 10-minute window at the start for anonymous slips.

Recruitment: the librarian spends the first two weeks before launch contacting schools, youth sports clubs, after-school care centres and youth workers, asking them to post a flyer or announce the programme. Assumption: at least two of these bridge institutions will agree to host a sign-up table or announcement; if none does, sign-up moves to the branch's front desk and social media. Teens are invited to bring a friend. The message is 'make a thing, get a certificate, free snacks', not 'come read'.

Budget ($500 total): $150 for bulk snacks (about $25 per week for 12 teens, bought from a warehouse club). $100 for low-cost maker supplies such as cardboard, tape, printed backgrounds and recycled props. $100 for printing: posters, flyers, sign-up slips and the final zine. $150 reserve for circuit kits, replacement supplies or a late-stage overrun. Assumption: the branch's existing tablets and free apps cover recording and animation, so no software is bought.

Outcome measures beyond attendance: first, a single-page pre and post survey in weeks 1 and 6 asking about reading confidence and enjoyment on a 1 to 5 scale, with an anonymous self-chosen code so pairs can be matched. Second, a project-quality rubric scored by the librarian on each finished artefact (completion, a written component, and a presentation), tracked across weeks. Third, library card sign-ups and any item borrowed in the six weeks, drawn from circulation records. Fourth, a recommend-to-a-friend question in the week 6 survey. The manager reads as evidence of change a rise of at least one point on the reading-confidence scale for at least half of paired completers, with card sign-ups among non-visitors. Because a six-week pilot cannot prove causation, the manager should treat this as a signal to repeat, not as proof.

Fit to four librarian hours a week: 1 hour on Tuesday for preparation and tech checks; 1.5 hours on Thursday for the session, including the 10-minute slip window; 1.5 hours on Friday for admin, sorting slips and planning the next week. Assumption: this uses all four hours with no spare time, so any outreach beyond the first two weeks must be done by volunteers. Volunteers are drawn from a teen advisory board or local university students in education or media; they handle snacks, equipment setup and supervision, but do not take on recruitment or data entry.
